'''Martin F. Semmelhack''' (born November 19, 1941) is an American organic chemist and Professor of Chemistry at [[Princeton University]]. His research career focuses on the application of [[transition metal]] chemistry to [[organic synthesis]], developing new [[organonickel chemistry|organonickel-]] and palladium-catalyzed methodology, including the palladium-catalyzed cyclization known as the Semmelhack reaction. He has also researched reactions of [[Transition metal arene complex|arene-]] and [[Transition metal complexes of dienes, trienes, and tetraenes|diene-metal complexes]]. In the later part of his career his research turned toward chemical biology, particularly the study of bacterial [[quorum sensing]] in collaboration with Princeton molecular biologist [[Bonnie Bassler]]. 

According to fellow Princeton chemist [[David MacMillan]], Semmelhack is "an elder statesman” of organometallic chemistry, recognized for "pushing chemical synthesis into conceptually novel areas."<ref name="cen">{{cite magazine |title=Arthur C. Cope Scholar: Martin F. Semmelhack |magazine=Chemical & Engineering News |volume=91 |issue=9 |date=2013 |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/91/i9/Arthur-C-Cope-Scholar-Martin.html |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Semmelhack was born on November 19, 1941, in [[Appleton, Wisconsin]], where he was raised.<ref name="bio">{{cite web |title=Biography |url=https://www.princeton.edu/~mfshack/bio.html |website=Semmelhack Laboratory, Princeton University Department of Chemistry |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref><ref name="cen" /> Developing an early enthusiasm for chemistry as a teenager, he periodically visited the stockroom of nearby [[Lawrence University|Lawrence College]] to request chemicals—including concentrated [[sulfuric acid]], supplied only with written permission from Semmelhack's mother—for experiments he conducted with borrowed glassware in his parents' basement.<ref name="cen" />

He attended the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] from 1959 to 1963, earning a Bachelor of Science degree in chemistry, and worked as an undergraduate on organic photochemistry with [[Howard Zimmerman|Howard E. Zimmerman]].<ref name="cv">{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae |url=https://www.princeton.edu/~mfshack/cv.html |website=Semmelhack Laboratory, Princeton University Department of Chemistry |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref><ref name="bio" /> A young member of the Wisconsin faculty, [[David M. Lemal]], became a mentor and friend, advising Semmelhack to pursue doctoral study with a young colleague at Harvard whose work he described as "really exciting," [[E. J. Corey]].<ref name="cen" />

Following Lemal's advice, Semmelhack began doctoral study at [[Harvard University]] in the fall of 1963, joining Corey's group to work in the then-new field of organotransition-metal reagents applied to organic synthesis.<ref name="bio" /><ref name="cv" /> He received an A.M. in 1965 and a Ph.D. in organic chemistry in 1967.<ref name="cv" /> He then held a [[National Institutes of Health]] postdoctoral fellowship at [[Stanford University]] under [[William Summer Johnson]], where he took part in work completing the first total synthesis of a natural steroid using a [[biomimetic synthesis|biomimetic]] [[polyolefin]] cyclization strategy.<ref name="bio" /><ref name="cv" />

== Academic career ==

In the fall of 1968, Semmelhack joined the chemistry faculty of [[Cornell University]] as an assistant professor.<ref name="cv" /><ref name="bio" /> He was promoted to associate professor in 1974 and to full professor in 1977.<ref name="cv" /> In 1978, he moved to [[Princeton University]] as professor of chemistry, a position he continues to hold as of 2026.<ref name="chemfaculty">{{cite web |title=Martin F. Semmelhack |url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty-research/faculty/martin-f-semmelhack/ |website=Princeton University Department of Chemistry |date=7 July 2025 |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref><ref name="rockefeller">{{cite web |title=Martin Semmelhack |url=https://rockefellercollege.princeton.edu/people/martin-semmelhack |website=Rockefeller College, Princeton University |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref> He served as associate chair of the chemistry department from 1993 to 1996.<ref name="cv" /> As of 2023, he was still teaching Princeton's introductory organic chemistry sequence, working alongside colleague Erik Sorensen to adapt the course to changing student preparation and needs.<ref name="paw">{{cite magazine |author=Keatley, Susan Reslewic |title=Higher Educating |magazine=Princeton Alumni Weekly |volume=124 |issue=3 |date=October 31, 2023 |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/article/higher-educating |access-date=July 16, 2026}}</ref> 

From 1988 to 1990, Semmelhack spent two years in industry, serving first as acting department head of the metabolic diseases section and then as consulting director of chemistry at the [[American Cyanamid]] Medical Research Division.<ref name="cv" /><ref name="bio" /><ref name="cen" />

In 2018, his fortieth year at Princeton, Semmelhack received the university's President's Award for Distinguished Teaching.<ref name="Teaching Award">{{cite web |last1=Dienst |first1=Karin |title=Four faculty members recognized for outstanding teaching |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2018/06/05/four-faculty-members-recognized-outstanding-teaching |website=Princeton University |publisher=The Trustees of Princeton University |access-date=17 July 2026}}</ref> Since 2014, the chemistry department has held a lecture series, the Semmelhack Symposia, in his honor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Special Symposia |url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/special-symposia/ |website=Department of Chemistry |publisher=Trustees of Princeton University |access-date=17 July 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

Across his career, Semmelhack's research has been characterized by the search for new reactivity, particularly in transition-metal-mediated processes, and its application to the synthesis of structurally complex or biologically active molecules.<ref name="cen" />

=== Organometallic methodology ===

Semmelhack's contributions lie in the development and application of transition metal complexes—principally chromium, nickel, and palladium species—as reagents and catalysts in organic synthesis. Semmelhack systematically expanded the synthetic utility of arene–chromium tricarbonyl complexes, demonstrating that these complexes activate arene rings toward nucleophilic addition, enabling transformations that were previously inaccessible through classical methods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Clark |first2=G. R. |last3=Garcia |first3=J. L. |last4=Harrison |first4=J. J. |last5=Thebtaranonth |first5=Y. |last6=Wulff |first6=W. |last7=Yamashita |first7=A. |title=Addition of carbon nucleophiles to arene-chromium complexes |journal=Tetrahedron |date=1981 |volume=37 |issue=23 |pages=3957–3965 |doi=10.1016/S0040-4020(01)93270-3}}</ref>

His early investigations at Cornell into the reactivity of zerovalent nickel complexes with aryl and vinyl halides described nickel-mediated coupling processes and provided early preparative routes to polyarene natural products, including alnusone.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Ryono |first2=Lauri S. |title=Nickel-promoted synthesis of cyclic biphenyls. Total synthesis of alnusone dimethyl ether |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1975 |volume=97 |issue=13 |pages=3873–3875 |doi=10.1021/ja00846a084 |bibcode=1975JAChS..97.3873S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Helquist |first2=Paul |last3=Jones |first3=L. D. |last4=Keller |first4=Leonard |last5=Mendelson |first5=L. |last6=Ryono |first6=Laurine Speltz |last7=Gorzynski Smith |first7=Janice |last8=Stauffer |first8=R. D. |title=Reaction of aryl and vinyl halides with zerovalent nickel—preparative aspects and the synthesis of alnusone |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1981 |volume=103 |issue=21 |pages=6460–6471 |doi=10.1021/ja00411a034 |bibcode=1981JAChS.103.6460S }}</ref> In the early 1980s, a [[annulation|benzannulation]] reaction of carbene–chromium complexes became a research focus, including its first intramolecular example, applied in a synthesis of the [[naphthoquinone]] antibiotic deoxyfrenolicin.<ref name="bio" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Bozell |first2=Joseph J. |title=The synthesis of nanaomycin A and deoxyfrenolicin by alkyne cycloaddition to chromium-carbene complexes |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1982 |volume=104 |issue=21 |pages=5850–5852 |doi=10.1021/ja00385a079 |bibcode=1982JAChS.104.5850S }}</ref>

In 2013, [[Stephen L. Buchwald]] of MIT praised Semmelhack's early recognition of transition metals' synthetic potential, calling Semmelhack "someone who was ahead of his time."<ref name="cen" />

=== The Semmelhack reaction ===

In the course of his benzannulation work, Semmelhack discovered a method to simplify the deoxyfrenolicin synthesis using an intramolecular, palladium(II)-catalyzed alkoxycarbonylation. The method he went on to develop for building [[tetrahydrofuran]] and [[tetrahydropyran]] rings is today known as the Semmelhack reaction.<ref name="bio" /><ref name="csr" /> In 1984, Semmelhack and Christina Bodurow applied this method to alcohols bearing pendant olefins: intramolecular oxypalladation forms a cyclic alkylpalladium intermediate that is carbonylated and then trapped, typically by methanol, to give a β-alkoxy [[ester]], with the resulting Pd(0) reoxidized ''in situ'' by CuCl<sub>2</sub> so that the reaction turns over catalytically in palladium.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=Martin F. |last2=Bodurow |first2=Christina |title=Intramolecular alkoxypalladation/carbonylation of alkenes |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1984 |volume=106 |issue=5 |pages=1496–1498 |doi=10.1021/ja00317a059 |bibcode=1984JAChS.106.1496S }}</ref><ref name="csr" /> A companion paper the same year showed that, using stoichiometric Pd(OAc)<sub>2</sub> and an internal alcohol nucleophile, intramolecular trapping of the intermediate acylpalladium species could instead construct two rings—a fused bicyclic lactone—in a single operation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Bodurow |first2=Christina |last3=Baum |first3=Mary |title=Direct synthesis of pyran-lactones related to naphthoquinone antibiotics |journal=Tetrahedron Letters |year=1984 |volume=25 |issue=30 |pages=3171–3174 |doi=10.1016/S0040-4039(01)91000-7}}</ref><ref name="csr" />

A 2021 tutorial review in ''Chemical Society Reviews'' discussed the Semmelhack reaction as one of a handful of palladium-catalyzed cascade cyclizations that have expedited complex natural product total synthesis, citing applications including Tang and Werness's synthesis of (−)-kumausallene, in which a gram-scale Semmelhack reaction served as the fourth step of the route, and Tang, Chen, and Yang's synthesis of (±)-schindilactone A, in which the reaction was instead used late-stage, on a fully elaborated pentacyclic intermediate, to forge two of the natural product's eight rings.<ref name="csr" />

=== Spiroconjugation ===

Semmelhack's group at Cornell prepared spiro[4.4]nonatetraene, providing one of the first experimental test cases for [[Conjugated system|spiroconjugation]]—the through-space electronic interaction between two π systems joined at a common ''sp''<sup>3</sup>-hybridized spiro carbon.<ref name="bio" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Foos |first2=J. S. |last3=Katz |first3=S. |title=Spiro [4.4] nonatetraene and spiro [4.4] nona-1, 3, 7-triene. Synthesis and properties. Effects of spiroconjugation |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1973 |volume=95 |issue=22 |pages=7325–7336 |doi=10.1021/ja00803a021 |bibcode=1973JAChS..95.7325S }}</ref>

=== TEMPO oxidation and electrocatalysis ===

Semmelhack developed [[TEMPO]] as a reagent for selective oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes. Subsequent work showed that TEMPO functions as a mediator for the electrooxidation of primary [[amines]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Chou |first2=C. S. |last3=Cortes |first3=D. A. |title=Nitroxyl-mediated electrooxidation of alcohols to aldehydes and ketones |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1983 |volume=105 |issue=13 |pages=4492–4494 |doi=10.1021/ja00351a070 |bibcode=1983JAChS.105.4492S }}</ref> By running this reaction under aqueous conditions, primary amines were converted to aldehydes, while under anhydrous conditions they were converted to nitriles.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Schmid |first2=C. R. |title=Nitroxyl-Mediated Electro-oxidation of Amines to Nitriles and Carbonyl Compounds |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1983 |volume=105 |issue=22 |pages=6732–6734 |doi=10.1021/ja00360a042 |bibcode=1983JAChS.105.6732S }}</ref> In related work, the selective TEMPO oxidation reaction was shown to work selectively with Cu(II) as a catalyst and oxygen as the stoichiometric oxidant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Schmid |first2=C. R. |last3=Cortes |first3=D. A. |last4=Chou |first4=C. S. |title=Oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes with oxygen and cupric ion, mediated by nitrosonium ion |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1984 |volume=106 |issue=11 |pages=3374–3376 |doi=10.1021/ja00323a064}}</ref> This process was refined and generalized by Shannon Stahl and is known as the [[Stahl Oxidation]].

Semmelhack also developed electrochemical methods for organic synthesis, including protocols for selective protecting-group removal by electro-reduction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semmelhack |first1=M. F. |last2=Heinsohn |first2=G. E. |title=Selective removal of protecting groups using controlled potential electrolysis |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1972 |volume=94 |issue=14 |pages=5139–5140 |doi=10.1021/ja00769a087}}</ref><ref name="csr">{{cite journal |last1=Holman |first1=Karli R. |last2=Stanko |first2=Allison M. |last3=Reisman |first3=Sarah E. |title=Palladium-catalyzed cascade cyclizations involving C–C and C–X bond formation: strategic applications in natural product synthesis |journal=Chemical Society Reviews |year=2021 |volume=50 |issue=14 |pages=7891–7908 |doi=10.1039/d0cs01385d |pmid=34037626 }}</ref>

=== Quorum sensing and chemical biology ===

In the later part of his career, in collaboration with Princeton molecular biologist [[Bonnie Bassler]] and others, his group has focused on the phenomenon of [[quorum sensing]], a form of bacterial cell-to-cell communication mediated by diffusible small-molecule signaling compounds known as autoinducers.<ref name="chemfaculty" /><ref name="cen" /> In addition to characterizing and synthesizing the natural signals, Semmelhack's group designed, synthesized, and evaluated small-molecule [[agonists]] and [[receptor antagonist|antagonists]] as chemical probes of the quorum-sensing circuits of human pathogens including ''[[Vibrio cholerae]]'', ''[[Pseudomonas aeruginosa]]'', and ''[[Staphylococcus aureus]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Higgins |first1=D. A. |last2=Pomianek |first2=M. E. |last3=Kraml |first3=C. M. |last4=Taylor |first4=R. K. |last5=Semmelhack |first5=M. F. |last6=Bassler |first6=B. L. |title=The major Vibrio cholerae autoinducer and its role in virulence factor production |journal=Nature |date=6 December 2007 |volume=450 |issue=7171 |pages=883–886 |doi=10.1038/nature06284 |pmid=18004304 |bibcode=2007Natur.450..883H }}</ref><ref name="Bassler">{{cite journal |last1=O'Loughlin |first1=C. T. |last2=Miller |first2=L. C. |last3=Siryaporn |first3=A. |last4=Drescher |first4=K. |last5=Semmelhack |first5=M. F. |last6=Bassler |first6=B. L. |title=A quorum-sensing inhibitor blocks Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence and biofilm formation |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |year=2013 |volume=110 |issue=44 |pages=17981–17986 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1316981110 |doi-access=free |pmid=24143808 |pmc=3816427 |bibcode=2013PNAS..11017981O }}</ref> These molecules have been studied as potential anti-virulence therapeutics that act without directly killing the bacteria, an approach intended to reduce the selective pressure that drives antibiotic resistance.<ref name="chemfaculty" /><ref name="Bassler" />

== Professional service ==

Semmelhack has served on the editorial or advisory boards of the ''[[Journal of Organic Chemistry]]'', ''[[Organometallics]]'', ''[[Organic Reactions]]'', and ''[[Organic Syntheses]]''.<ref name="bio" /> Within the [[American Chemical Society]], he served on the Executive Committee of the Division of Organic Chemistry and was chair of the division in 1988.<ref name="cv" /><ref name="cen" />
